There have long been rumors and speculation that Apple is developing a foldable clamshell device, which could be an iPad, a Mac, one of each, or a hybrid of the two.

A recent report suggests that although this project was once a priority for incoming CEO John Ternus, it has ultimately been canceled — but I don’t think that’s entirely accurate…

As for me, the concept of a Mac and iPad hybrid has essentially been made obsolete by the times. Today’s Macs can run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many of us, iPhone Mirroring is another tool that achieves the same thing. We’re also seeing increasing convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe this trend will continue: Apple’s old argument that convergence would mean "merging a refrigerator and a toaster" is firmly a thing of the past.

That said, I do believe that one day we’ll have a full-screen foldable Mac — provided the technology can fully replace a physical keyboard with a software one. This won’t happen in the short term, but it will eventually happen.

Medium-term stage: dynamic keyboard

I think there’s still a long way to go, because there will be an interim phase: the emergence of a dynamic hardware keyboard. I discussed nearly a decade ago why I believed this was the way forward. Although such technology is already used in certain niche applications, it has yet to enter the mainstream market.

The Sonder Keyboard was one of the early attempts, using tiny e-ink displays to redefine key labels and functions.

For example, for a user who spends the whole day editing in Final Cut Pro, a QWERTY keyboard is virtually useless, which is why both physical keyboards and keyboard covers exist on the market.

How clever would it be if our MacBook keyboard or desktop Magic Keyboard could automatically change its labels according to whichever app is currently in use?

A software keyboard that feels like a hardware one

However, the long-term goal has always been a full software keyboard. Back in 2016, I noted that the same argument Steve Jobs made about virtual keys when introducing the iPhone applies equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, software keyboards have three major problems:

  • A glass keyboard is uncomfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch typists need to feel a key before pressing it

Apple already has patents addressing each of these three issues. First, using a flexible display instead of conventional glass allows virtual keys to deform when pressed. The second problem can be solved by combining this deformation with haptic motors. Finally, regarding whether one can feel physical keys with a fingertip, there are two solutions.

Apple’s patent uses electrostatic charges to make people feel changes in surface texture. In other words, even if the surface remains flat, charges applied to the display surface can give the sensation of physical keys. In 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University proposed another solution.

It’s only a matter of time, not whether it will happen

Of course, all of these technologies are still at a very early stage, but we only need to look at the Mac trackpad to know there is precedent. Trackpads today still sound and feel like mechanical devices, but in reality they have been solid-state devices simulating physical clicks through haptic technology for years — and the effect is remarkably convincing.

Software keyboards will eventually reach the same level of maturity. Whether using Apple’s currently proposed approach, or technologies not yet seen, they will solve the three major problems mentioned above.

When that day comes, Steve’s argument will apply equally to the Mac. In clamshell mode, the keyboard will take on the form best suited to the work at hand. When we just need one giant display, whether for watching movies or drawing with Apple Pencil, we can unfold it into a double-sized screen.

So I fully accept that the first-generation product may have been shelved for now, but that absolutely does not mean it has been canceled. The technology will eventually come into its own.

Those are my thoughts — what do you think? Feel free to share in the comments.
